clause_name: Article IV, Section 1 — Termination of Agreement (para. A)
label: POSITIVE
reasoning_cat1: Standing alone the wording is definite and mechanical: an identified party ('Core Physician'), an identified right ('may terminate this Agreement'), an express standard ('without cause'), a fixed period ('ninety (90) days'), a required form ('prior written notice') and a named recipient ('County'). No term carries two reasonable meanings; 'without cause' is a term of art whose whole function is to remove any cause inquiry. There is no general catch-all sitting against enumerated specifics. The only intrinsic oddity is that the paragraph is labelled 'A' with no 'B', but a lettering stub is not itself a lexical or scope ambiguity.
reasoning_cat2: Read against the rest of the instrument this provision will not sit still. Article IV is captioned 'TERMINATION AND CORRECTIVE ACTION' and this is its entire section 1; section 2 is missing from the instrument and section 3 then presupposes 'the decision to impose corrective action or terminate for cause' - a decision no operative provision of this Agreement authorises anyone to make. So the only express termination right in the article captioned for termination runs one way, to the physician, while the County's termination rights surface piecemeal and on inconsistent terms elsewhere: Art. V sec. 6 (immediate termination for a pre-existing conflict of interest), Art. V sec. 13 (Agreement 'may be immediately terminated', agent unnamed, on restriction of privileges) and Art. V sec. 15 (30 days' notice on non-appropriation). Against Art. I sec. 1's fixed five-year term to October 4, 2007 and Art. V sec. 11's cumulative-remedies reservation to County, a court must decide whether the County has any at-will or for-cause termination power at all, and if so on what notice - exactly the kind of gap that cannot be harmonised by reading the instrument as a whole.

clause_name: Article V, Section 11 — Enforcement of Remedies
label: POSITIVE
reasoning_cat1: Two intrinsic features. First, the clause closes an enumeration with an open catch-all: 'by law or in equity or by statute or otherwise' - 'or otherwise' has no ascertainable boundary once law, equity and statute are already named, and invites the ejusdem generis / expressio unius dispute. Second, and more sharply, the drafting is entirely one-directional: it preserves and accumulates rights and remedies 'conferred on or reserved to County' only, and says nothing about the physician's remedies, so any genuine ambiguity in its reach would ordinarily be resolved against the County as drafter. The clause also assumes a stock of remedies 'herein conferred on or reserved to County' whose content it never identifies.
reasoning_cat2: The premise of the clause is that the Agreement confers remedies on County, but Article IV - the article devoted to termination and corrective action - confers no express remedy or termination right on County at all (sec. 1.A runs only to the physician, and sec. 2 is absent), so the phrase 'herein conferred on or reserved to County' is partly without referent. Worse, 'may be enforced concurrently or from time to time' pulls directly against Art. IV sec. 3, which channels 'the decision to impose corrective action or terminate for cause' into the Faculty Practice Board's 'Corrective Action and Termination Review Process' or the medical staff bylaws, 'whichever is applicable': one provision says County may pursue every remedy concurrently and at will, the other conditions the principal remedies on a mandatory review-and-appeal procedure. It also sits uneasily with Art. V sec. 4, which forbids construing any provision against its drafter while sec. 11 is drafted wholly in County's favour, and it overlaps Art. V sec. 17's non-waiver reservation without either yielding to the other.

clause_name: Royalties, Quantity and Payments \u2014 Section 2(b) (projected manufacturing quantities)
label: POSITIVE
reasoning_cat1: The operative verb phrase "projects to manufacture at least" is genuinely susceptible of two reasonable constructions. "Projects" is the language of forecast or estimate — a non-binding statement of expectation — while "at least" is the language of a binding floor or minimum commitment. A reader cannot tell from the clause's own words whether Licensee has undertaken an enforceable minimum-volume obligation or merely stated a business projection. Compounding this, the numbers are tied to "manufacture," not to sale, so even on the binding reading it is unclear what is promised: units made, or units moved. The clause also supplies no consequence for falling short, leaving the promissory character of "projects" undetermined on its face. This is the same species of defect the Hartford court found in "premises"/"person"/"occupy": a term that on ordinary usage bears more than one reasonable meaning, each of which a party can fairly advance.
reasoning_cat2: Section 2(d) requires fixed monthly payments of $16,313 / $19,031 / $23,562, which are precisely the projected quantities multiplied by the $0.87 Royalty Rate of §2(a) and divided by twelve (225,000 × $0.87 ÷ 12 = $16,312.50). Section 2(e) then computes an "Excess Payment" on Products *sold* "in excess of the projected amount for that year set forth in section (b)" — treating (b)'s manufacturing projections as a sales baseline. Section 2(f) speaks of an aggregate 812,500 units "for which payment had already been made," which is the sum of the three (b) figures. So the rest of Section 2 operates as though (b) fixed binding minimums measured in sales, while (b) itself says only that Licensee "projects to manufacture." Section 5(d) reinforces the tension by contrasting the (d)/(e) regime with a fallback of "no minimum quantities required," implying the ordinary regime does impose minimums. Pulling the other way, §14(g) disclaims any guarantee as to sales activity. Harmonising all of these still leaves a genuine internal inconsistency about whether (b) is a commitment or a forecast, and whether it is measured by manufacture or by sale.

clause_name: Royalties, Quantity and Payments \u2014 Section 2(i) (Best Efforts Provision)
label: POSITIVE

The compound "good faith, best efforts" is itself uncertain: it may state one hybrid standard or two cumulative ones, and "best efforts" is variously construed as anything from ordinary diligence to a near-fiduciary exertion. The object, "all Products manufactured," is definite enough. Standing alone the clause is vague but not incoherent, and courts routinely enforce best-efforts covenants, so this sits below the flagging line — the real problem is relational, not intrinsic.
reasoning_cat2: This provision is squarely contradicted by §14(g), which states that Licensee "makes no guarantees, representations, warranties, or promises regarding its sales activity of the Product and shall in its sole discretion devote as much or as little (or none) of its time and resources to selling the Product." One clause imposes an affirmative best-efforts duty to market and sell; the other disclaims any promise about sales and reserves absolute discretion to devote nothing. These cannot both be given full force: a party who devotes none of its resources to selling has by definition not used best efforts. This is the Roadlink pattern — a broad disclaimer sitting against an affirmative quality/performance undertaking elsewhere in the same instrument, with no conditional language subordinating one to the other, and no "notwithstanding" clause resolving priority (contrast §2(h) and §2(j), which do carry such language). The tension is aggravated by §2(b)/(e), whose volume projections presuppose active selling effort.
